title: 2026/09/03 - PP
machineSummary: MPI and DOC officials said three wild bird flu cases are detected, with no poultry cases. Officials said NAWAC is consulting on welfare code changes. DOC is vaccinating endangered species, costing $150,000 for tranche one administration. BirdCare and councils are coordinating on emergency triage and carcass disposal.

chunks.text: Thanks for coming at reasonable short notice. I guess we're looking for a bit of an update, and I know that the various members of the committee do have some questions. So, we're in your hands. Perfect. Manny, do you want to just give a little bit of an update?

Of course. So we haven't found any further detections. So that is still the current state. So three detections in the Wellington bottom of the south, sorry, South of the North Island region. All of those in wild birds, one of them in the carrier, two in pelagic seabirds, ones that come from the Southern Ocean and then make landfall in either or Australia. Still the situation.

Surveillance continues. Public still continue to report to the exotic pest and disease hotline, which we're very grateful for. Surveillance continues at the various wildlife hospitals and those we'll run through to the exotic pest and disease hotline as required. No detections in poultry, and the readiness activities with the poultry industry continue to progress. So.

Right. So we'll go to questions. Yeah. Yeah. Thank you, Chair. Thank you. I just wanted to touch base about the correspondence, about the rules around hens. Mm-hmm. And obviously, NAWAC is undertaking their review of the Code of Welfare, and that they are proposing that to be permanent.

Yes, my concern is that, it appears from the correspondence that the reason they're proposing that is because there isn't an opportunity to make a temporary change, in the case of a biosecurity incident. I guess my question is, we're currently, and we've just had the committee stage of the Emergency Management Bill. This could potentially be included in that bill, potentially.

So I'd be interested in whether you sought any advice on whether it would be considered, because a biosecurity outbreak can potentially be part of emergency management. And so whether any advice was sought on whether that would've been a better mechanism to use so that you can make a temporary adjustment. Because no one, I think, disagrees that there will be times when you need to make a temporary adjustment.

But it seems it's at odds with our animal welfare obligations to be making a permanent adjustment. So what I'm interested in is whether any advice was sought on other legal mechanisms that could've been used so that a temporary adjustment could be made. Lisa, do you want me to touch on that?

Yeah, I can do that. So I guess that I would open by saying that our Animal Welfare Act in New Zealand sets minimum expectations for the way we look after animals. So, looking to adjust those lower than the minimum isn't something that we have generally spent a lot of time on.

So, the kind of concept of allowing inappropriate treatment of animals in certain circumstances is not something that is built into the Animal Welfare Act. That said, we do have mechanisms to manage the biosecurity elements of incidents. I think if we separate that question from the question about the hens, so NAWAC's-- there's kind of two elements to their deliberations around the hens code elements. One is the fact that, on reviewing the science, they have decided, and to consult on

changing the standard for the stocking density to nine hens per square meter because they consider that science does not support seven, and seven is certainly out of step with all other standards around the world. So they are saying, in their view, nine is an appropriate minimum standard for New Zealand's animal welfare.

And so there is no need then to look at any sort of a temporary change. The second element is the fact that bird flu has arrived. We're expecting it'll become an endemic disease in New Zealand, as with everywhere else. And the decisions about management of stock in any case where we have endemic diseases is for the owner of that stock to make decisions on a case-by-case basis based on the risk. And the risk is dependent on a variety of things, including the environmental factors, what's happening around, but also the

mechanisms that that farmer uses to manage their stock. So at the moment, we have a variety of approaches taken by different layer hen producers, based on their personal appetite for business loss as well as their normal operations and their management of risk.

So we would expect to see those kinds of decisions being taken independently by individual operators on an ongoing basis. And so decisions to bring birds in or out will be taken in that way rather than controlled by a central government or other central kind of decision maker. So I guess, I've got a few follow-up questions.

So while I appreciate this is NAWAC's approach is and not MPI's itself, I guess I would assume that they would be seeking some advice or some secretarial support from MPI. Mm-hmm. My question is, the top of the letter that you wrote to us said that what triggered this, though, was the bird flu.

This is what triggered the discussion point. And so my question was quite specific. What other options did you look at in terms of trying to address this? So was there advice sought on whether a large-scale outbreak would meet the criteria for emergency management? So yes, Emergency Management is its own act, but there are a range of different types of emergencies that can occur that can then trigger emergency management, and it doesn't have to be a natural disaster.

COVID, for example, was a health emergency. Mm-hmm. So my question is- Yeah... did you seek that as an option instead so that you can make a temporary adjustment rather than actually having a permanent change to the Code of Welfare? Well, like I say, the concept of temporary reductions in animal welfare is not something that MPI is generally seeking, and nor our go-to policy response.

We do think that biosecurity risk can be managed in ways without compromising animal welfare. So the concept itself is not our usual go-to. In this case, the request to NAWAC was triggered from the minister. He sought a specific and kind of quick turnaround compared to the more standard, fuller, longer process to look specifically at elements that might allow for movement of hens, and the trigger was the bird flu.

That doesn't change NAWAC's process, which is that they must consider the science. So they looked at a range of options when they started to consider the issue, and my understanding is that they considered a temporary option, and their view was, like I said, because of the expectation this disease will become endemic and that decisions will need to be made on a very localized basis, and that there's an element there of the individual business decision around risk appetite and so on, that it wasn't a suitable kind of an activity for there to be a

central controller of that. So- And we'll-- Sorry. We'll also obviously review both the consultation ourselves, and I think the complexity, it's a good question round about what parts of the act for emergencies, but animal welfare remains the primary consideration. Then there's the resilience whilst preparing for the potential that it will be endemic in the space. So we have to look at that factor for the poultry industry in terms of resilience in the future.

And then the third thing is about resilience and food security. So you've got all the competing factors of that to get the balance right. NAWAC's, as Lisa said, looked at the current code and have provided the consultation document to look at, but we'll also balance that as well as we always do in terms of our advice to the minister.

The challenge from my perspective will be around about if it does get into poultry, then what's the potential benefits and trade-offs of an emergency solution rather than a full-time solution that covers all of what I've just said, the animal welfare, making sure we're prepared for HPAI and make sure we limit the spread where we can, but also the resilience in food security.

So I've got a couple questions. One is, so if you've got hens packed in closer together, doesn't that potentially make the spread, like actually make the spread happen more, like go faster? Doesn't that increase the risk of spread or- No. In a situation, if animals are densely housed and biosecurity is poor, then that is indeed the case, that densely housed animals will spread between themselves.

The industry is working on improving biosecurity so that the disease can stay out of sheds, and that is literally one of the only things that they can do, is to increase biosecurity at the shed and farm level to stop the disease coming in. So why does making them more densely contained help as a response to bird flu?

Well, I can probably answer that. I think it's less about the more densely contained, and it's more about the fact that at the moment we have two different standards. One for birds and layer hens that have access to an outdoor area during the day, and a second standard for layer hens that do not have access to an outdoor area.

So at the moment, the standard for layer hens that do not have access to the outdoor area is seven, and for those that do have it's nine. And the nine was decided to do with the fact that at certain times of the day, the hens have a bigger space to access. So like I say, the science is being reviewed, and it's considered that nine is a sufficient amount of space. I think the link to the HPAI is the fact that if you have outdoors-living birds, that they are mixing in and out and they have the nine requirement, at the moment under the

code, you wouldn't just be allowed to move all of those birds inside your shed and keep them inside until you felt it was appropriate to let them out. That's right. Because then you would have this nine stocking, but you would have birds living indoors. So at the moment, the farmers don't have that flexibility. They would need to cull birds or otherwise dispose of some birds in some other way, maybe to a friendly neighbor farm who's got some space or whatever. But they don't have that flexibility right now. So the purpose of allowing, of

aligning the standards was to allow flexibility and management to allow quick on-the-ground decisions. Just one final question. Last one. Yeah. Did you or did NAWAC seek advice around impact on the UK and EU free trade agreements, which have got animal welfare clauses in them, where New Zealand has said we will not reduce any of our animal welfare standards, and whether these changes could potentially breach- And I recognize that the UK and EU have got, that what we're proposing is more likely to match that, but that's not actually the

point. The point is that the agreements look at us reducing any of our regulations. So just wondering if any advice was sought on whether it would potentially breach any of the FTAs. I think MFAT are best placed to legal opinion on that. But as far as we're aware that there's no specific obligations under that NZ-EU ETA that would be impacted by this change.

But did you ask MFAT for advice on that? Not at this stage, but again, we'll continue in terms of through the consultation, through the process and our review and our advice back to the minister. Do the officials have any- Just going to say at this point, it's not my responsibility to consider that. That'll be an obligation for us as we advise the minister around the code if it's reported back.

So we'll need to have that conversation with our MFAT and our trade international colleague. Yeah. Sue's had a question. Oh, you sort of answered it, but triggered another one maybe. So is this basically free-range birds that are then going to be required to be kept inside? Is that essentially what you're talking about? Or am I going on the wrong track?

That is essentially what we're talking about, but the decision to keep them inside is the businesses. So there's no requirement to keep your bird inside, but you may choose to do so in order to protect it. So no matter how bad it gets, it will always be up to the individual business owners to determine what to do. And then, for example, if they do decide to keep them inside, at what point are the eggs they produce no longer free-range?

It's a great Fair Trading Act question. And I believe that we have had some conversations with MB on that. And I think that Egg Industry is in conversations with the Commerce Commission around what's an appropriate correct labeling. Is that right? That's correct. Because last time when we met, I said that some of the actual egg farmers hadn't had a lot of feedback, that you guys had been talking to the industry, but it hadn't sort of trickled down.

And that was one of the questions that I did get asked, do they have to change their packaging? Should they be ordering packaging, or will it be okay to stick a label on it to say, "Actually, no." So we did have a webinar with all of the egg producers the other day. Fantastic. Thank you. And there was a discussion about this. There has been conversations with the Commerce Commission about this disease and the impacts it's had internationally and what the approaches there have been. The industry is also, they've showed me the stickers that they

have that they can stick on things. This is actually quite labor-intensive and difficult. Yes. And so there are ongoing conversations between the industry and supermarkets and the Commerce Commission. So this is definitely ongoing. We also, at that webinar, presented some maps showing testing in different places and had a discussion about how farmers might be able to interpret that testing and different detections to understand their risk when they make these decisions.

Steve. Thank you. Different line of questioning. We visited BirdCare Aotearoa recently, who were at pains to say that their main message was call the 800 number if you see any birds behaving strangely. They are a well-known location for people taking sick birds of all type.

They were previously bird rescue, and they're known sort of in the community beyond simply things that are communicated publicly, if you know what I mean. So their concern is they're wanting to set up some sort of triage at the gate for people who are going to turn up with sick birds, even though people have been told not to touch the birds.

Mm-hmm. They're concerned people won't follow those instructions, and they might either try and look after themselves and take them home and they're very much across the need to deal with the fundamental problem. But they're concerned that they don't have the ability to separate birds that haven't got the virus from ones that do, and that the public interacting with them will cause the problem to be worse.

I wonder, have you engaged with them directly, and are you able to support their call for some assistance in setting up a triage in West Auckland? That's the first question. And the second question is, there was a discussion about if this were to get into the gannet colony, for example, out at Muriwai or other places like that, and there would be a large-scale death toll, sadly.

Whether there was regarded as zero value in trying to deal with carcasses in an appropriate way to stop the spread because obviously other birds or other animals will come and interact with those carcasses. And it did strike me that in terms of stopping the curve of infection, not because we're going to eliminate it, but because we're going to try and break the curve, then is there some place for, in an instance like that, where you've got a large bird that lived potentially by a large populous area of humans and other animals, whether there's a place for large-scale

burials. And I know that on those Black Sound West Coast beaches of Whangamutoto, we bury whales and things, so we could bury a whole lot of birds. Two questions. Do you want to take them? Yes. Or do you want to talk about your engagement with the hospitals? Simon.

So for the rehab centers, we spoke to BirdCare Aotearoa the other day. Mm-hmm. There's about 46 rehab for birds around the country. Mm-hmm. So we've been talking to an initial 20, and we're ringing the others at the moment to work out what their needs are and how they're getting on at the moment. And Pretty positive feedback from most of them, actually.

They're managing all right at the moment. With BirdCare Aotearoa, they're really keen to set up that isolation unit, and that's obviously got a cost to it, and also some additional staff to help them work seven days a week. So we're working through how we could support them if we can, but also bearing in mind that there's another 45 that are also probably going to look for some help if we get into this stage.

Yeah. One option that we might look at is if we can offer some kind of grant scheme that people can apply for additional help. But obviously, early days on how we go about that at the moment. The other thing with the BirdCare establishment is it's one of the five wildlife hospitals that we have a contract with to do swabbing on a routine basis.

Mm-hmm. So we increased that contract earlier this year in anticipation of the additional work. Yeah. And we could also look at is there anything else in that contract arrangement that we could provide additional support for as well. Okay. Yeah. So we are working on this, and we do realize that although the advice might be leave birds where you find them and- Yeah... people are still going to want to help- Yeah... and still going to take birds somewhere.

So we have to accept that that's going to happen and provide support where we can. Yeah. As we move through this over the next few weeks, months, and it changes because we'll have a lot more birds, we'll have a lot more virus around, and it will change over time. So some of the rehab outfits have got to have a think about what's their operating model as they get busier moving forward.

Yeah. So we'll work that out as we go, I guess. It's hard to predict how different types of birds will react to the virus. On the- Sorry, the main point I think you've raised is that they're massively valuable to have a strong strategic partnership for this. They've already put, obviously, the value of two of the detections came through these rehab hospitals who are extremely conscious that we've got to work closely, take on board their feedback, and set up any partnerships that assist, including the discussion that Angus and the team had this week.

So we need to maintain that strong partnership with these providers as we continue to prepare and make sure that we're ready. Yeah. That's great to hear because I think there's a real resource there, and they're keen to help, and they're very well-connected in the local area.

Communities and- Yeah. All that stuff... volunteer organizations. Absolutely. Sorry. Do you want me to answer the disposal? Yes. So on the disposal side of things, it's a huge amount of work going on in that area across the board. So with mass die-offs, it depends really who the landowner is.

So it might be councils, it might be a private landowner, it might be DOC. Could be any of those. So we've got to work with them around what the most suitable way to either leave things where they are or dispose of them. If it's really accessible to the public, we might have a different approach to one that nobody ever gets to. So we did a webinar this morning with, I think there was about 140 people from all the councils looking at composting.

So that's an option that might be a real easy way to dispose of large numbers of birds, particularly poultry. But also, if we get large die-offs of seals or that kind of thing. Yeah. Mm-hmm. But we're looking at every option is kind of what I'm saying, whether that's burial on site where they are, burial somewhere else or landfill or whatever.

And that could minimize the spread somewhat. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Mary? So I think there's limited scientific information about if moving those things and burying them and having the people in and out to do that work is a plus or a minus in terms of spread. Right. So I think we just need to keep that in mind. Yeah. Certainly when we want to decrease the ability for people and pets and things to interact with them.

So in places where there is lots of traffic and things, obviously then these things become really important. But in terms of the scientific data about if burying everything or moving them actually helps or not- Yeah... I think the jury is pretty much out on that. Right. Okay. Yeah. Internationally although, yeah.

So in my electorate, Oamaru has a harbor with lots of native birds, shags, penguin seals, and if there was to be a large scale event, I imagine it would be several sites around the country, and MPI just won't be able to get to every site. So are you confident that the regional council, local council, and NGOs in those areas are able to deal with something like that? Because I'd assume the dead animals will have to be removed from the harbor in Oamaru

because you're going to have tourists and there's a lot of people there then. So I- And that's how you spread it too, right? Yeah, so. I spoke to Mayor Tuppendale, is it? Yeah. Yesterday, I think, so talking about exactly that situation where if they get a large number of animals around the harbor, how we can address that. So we're going to have a follow-up meeting.

She's going to bring all the council staff in. I think where we're going to get to is that it's best endeavors by all the partners- Yeah... and all the stakeholders. And if a particular council or landowner hasn't got the resources to deal with it, then we're going to have to have a look around the wider family and provide that support.

Okay. Yeah. And for those endangered species that we have, in my case it's yellow-eyed penguins, little blue penguins. There's others around the country that for wild animals will be reasonably easy to vaccinate because they're coming ashore into a nest every night.
How available are those vaccines for those different groups?

So at the moment, the vaccination program that DOC administers is under emergency- Use... use because of the, and the emergency is that the populations identified could become extinct at a national level. Yes. And Kat can take it from there.

Yeah. So at the moment, that's exactly the case. So for example, the korora is not on that list, and where we're at is- Yeah... where we're at is we will vaccinate those that are most at risk, and then the rest, it's the other measures that we can take. So really good biosecurity, good pest control, dog control, other things like that, that will impact on birds who will inevitably be impacted by the disease.

But the vaccination is a small part of that bigger picture for us. Just a very quick, so I understand, but are you saying you will vaccinate hoiho, for example? But regionally- When, yeah... yeah. Regionally also, little blue penguin may not be nationally threatened, but in a local area, if you lose the entire population, that has a very significant effect, because that population's gone.

Yeah. And in that region, it's gone. So are you thinking in those terms as well? Is there a scarcity of vaccine? Because it does seem in the case of little blue penguin, it would be great if regionally you could protect certain populations. Yeah. So again, it's very much at that extinction level that we're looking to protect because it's only one small tool and actually the things that are more effective are the other measures that you can take. So, I think there's a risk that we could say vaccinating is going to fix this

problem. The answer is it's absolutely not. Mm. It's very much a backstop for us for those species that are most at risk. So at a local level, what we're telling people, and we've also held a number of webinars, I think we've held six so far. We've had up to 400 people on some of those calls from wildlife centers, et cetera, around the country.

But very much the message is it's those other things that you can do that will be most effective, particularly for those local populations where we know birds are at risk. Because it doesn't work on chicks, does it? They've got to be a certain age, don't they, the animals, before you can get- So we can vaccinate birds with the current vaccines that we have.

They need one injection in one month. So start here, whatever age they are. Then a month later. Yep. And then after six months, and then, so this is an ongoing repeatable process. I just need to stress as well, it doesn't stop them from getting the disease. No. Mm-hmm. And so we don't know then if they are going to be completely protected or not, right? We also don't know if they will still be able to pass it to another bird, okay? Even if they don't die themselves.

Yeah. And so- And you would expect they would, though... you're just keeping them alive, but they're still infectious. That's possible. Similar to humans with influenza, right? Right. Exactly the same, and so that is the situation that we have, which is why this is a limited tool when we're talking about critically endangered species at the national level where every individual counts.

It's also very invasive. So- Yeah... if you're going into a wild bird population, capturing, that's quite a stressful situation. And then you have to recapture again the same bird six months later. But it's worth risk we've taken for hoiho. For, yeah, for particularly takahe, kaki, kakapo. Those birds, for kakapo, for example, they're all tagged.

We know exactly where they are. We know we can go there once. We know we can go back and get them again. And when you've only got a couple of hundred birds, it's vital that we've got some protected. Yeah. And how much per shot? That's the next question. The cost? Yeah. So I think the vaccine has been donated, so there is no cost for the vaccine.

But the cost comes- But there's a cost for the administration. That's correct. Yeah. So have you factored that in? Yep. Do you know how much yet? We have. So the exact figure is 100 and- 150,000 for tranche one... 150,000 for tranche one. What we've also been doing is training up a bit of a workforce of other people who can vaccinate, so people at wildlife centers, vets, et cetera, so that we're expanding the number of people and taking a bit of pressure off the small initial team.

So that's the first injection for all of those birds, tranche one? No, tranche one is-... bonus jabs for the five species that are part of tranche one. This is good value. So how many- Considering how hard it is to get species back. Yeah. It's because they're all captive. Yeah. Oh, gotcha. Thank you very much. Any further questions?

We've come to time, but thanks very much. I guess we could stress that it's really important to continue with your good work and to continue engaging with those communities and making sure that councils, et cetera, are actually talking to their NGOs as well. And ComCom- Yeah... feed back to the bird, the- Yeah, and I think the chicken, the poultry groups might be getting the information, but I don't know if every single farmer still is. So thank you.
Thank you very much. Thanks very much. Great. Mile. Thank you. See you again
